_about: Core changes in music, from the oldest instruments to 2050. year: number (negative = BCE). kind: sound (new sounds and instruments) | make (writing and making music) | listen (listening and sharing) | idea (what music is about). sure: firm | approx (date approximate) | legend (traditional attribution). tie: id of a track in soundtrack.json. Forecasts are editorial and built on the listed records.

records.title: Bone flutes
records.change: Flutes made from bird bone and mammoth ivory, found in caves of the Swabian Jura in Germany, are the oldest known musical instruments.
records.idea: Music is older than writing, farming and cities.

records.title: The oldest written melody
records.change: A clay tablet from Ugarit, in today’s Syria, carries the Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal, the oldest surviving substantially complete piece of notated music.
records.idea: Music can be written down and outlive the people who made it.

records.title: Harmony as number
records.change: Greek tradition credits Pythagoras with finding that pleasing intervals follow simple ratios: 2:1 for the octave, 3:2 for the fifth.
records.idea: Music is mathematics, and the cosmos itself has a harmony.
records.listen: Laurie Spiegel — Kepler’s Harmony of the Worlds
records.q: Laurie Spiegel Kepler's Harmony of the Worlds

records.title: A song on a gravestone
records.change: The Seikilos epitaph, carved on a grave marker in Asia Minor, is the oldest surviving complete piece of music, words and melody together.
records.idea: A song as a message across time: “While you live, shine.”

records.title: Gregorian chant and neumes
records.change: Church singers in the Frankish empire unify chant across a continent and begin writing it with neumes, signs that show the shape of a melody.
records.idea: Music as shared ritual: one melody sung the same way in many places.

records.title: The staff and do-re-mi
records.change: Guido of Arezzo writes notes on a staff of lines and teaches pitches with syllables, ut-re-mi, taken from a hymn.
records.idea: A trained singer can sing a melody they have never heard.

records.title: Four voices at once
records.change: At Notre-Dame in Paris, Pérotin writes “Viderunt omnes” for four independent voices.
records.idea: Polyphony: many independent lines can sound together and still make sense.

records.title: Printed music
records.change: Ottaviano Petrucci in Venice publishes the Odhecaton, the first book of polyphonic music printed with movable type.
records.idea: Music becomes a product that can be copied and sold.
records.listen: Josquin des Prez — chansons from the Odhecaton

records.title: Opera
records.change: Monteverdi’s L’Orfeo, staged in Mantua, sets a whole drama to music, a decade after the first operas in Florence.
records.idea: Music can tell a story and act out a drama.

records.title: Concerts for a paying public
records.change: Violinist John Banister starts concerts in London that anyone can attend by paying at the door.
records.idea: Music moves from church and court to anyone with a ticket.

records.title: The piano
records.change: Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence builds a keyboard with hammers, so the player’s touch controls soft and loud.
records.idea: Expression goes into the instrument.

records.title: Every key playable
records.change: Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier has a prelude and fugue in all 24 major and minor keys, played on one tuning.
records.idea: One tuning that works in every key lets music move freely between keys.
records.listen: Bach — Prelude and Fugue in C major, The Well-Tempered Clavier
records.q: Bach Well-Tempered Clavier Prelude C major

records.title: Beethoven’s Ninth
records.change: The first symphony by a major composer with vocal parts: its finale sets Schiller’s Ode to Joy, “Alle Menschen werden Brüder”.
records.idea: Music as a message to all humanity; today it is the anthem of Europe.

records.title: The oldest recorded voice
records.change: Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville traces a voice singing “Au clair de la lune” on soot-blackened paper. It is first played back in 2008.
records.idea: Sound can be stored.
records.q: Au clair de la lune 1860 phonautogram

records.title: The phonograph
records.change: Thomas Edison records sound on a tinfoil cylinder and plays it back.
records.idea: A performance can be repeated anywhere, without the musician.

records.title: Flat disc records
records.change: Emile Berliner’s gramophone plays flat discs that can be pressed by the thousand.
records.idea: Records become a mass product.

records.title: Noise as music
records.change: Futurist Luigi Russolo writes “The Art of Noises” and builds machines that roar and crackle. The same year Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring causes an uproar in Paris.
records.idea: Any sound, even an engine, can be music.

records.title: Jazz on record
records.change: The Original Dixieland Jass Band releases “Livery Stable Blues”, often called the first jazz record, and jazz spreads on disc.
records.idea: Improvisation: freedom inside a shared structure.

records.title: Radio
records.change: KDKA in Pittsburgh starts scheduled commercial broadcasting. Within a decade, radio brings music into millions of homes.
records.idea: Millions hear the same music at the same moment.

records.title: The theremin
records.change: Lev Termen in Soviet Russia builds an instrument played without touching it: the hands move in an electric field.
records.idea: Electricity makes new sounds, not just louder ones.

records.title: Twelve-tone music
records.change: Arnold Schoenberg arranges all twelve notes into rows and leaves the home key behind. Josef Matthias Hauer had published a similar method in 1919.
records.idea: Harmony without a home key.

records.title: Electrical recording
records.change: Microphones and amplifiers replace the acoustic recording horn.
records.idea: The microphone makes quiet, intimate singing possible.

records.title: The electric guitar
records.change: Rickenbacker’s “Frying Pan”, a cast-aluminium lap steel guitar, is among the first electric guitars with a magnetic pickup.
records.idea: A small band can be as loud as an orchestra.

records.title: Magnetic tape
records.change: AEG shows the Magnetophon tape recorder at the Berlin Radio Show. After the war, tape lets engineers cut, splice and overdub.
records.idea: A recording can be edited, so a performance can be built rather than captured.

records.title: Musique concrète
records.change: Pierre Schaeffer at French radio composes “Étude aux chemins de fer” from recorded train sounds.
records.idea: Recorded sound is raw material: the ancestor of sampling.
records.listen: Pierre Schaeffer — Étude aux chemins de fer
records.q: Pierre Schaeffer Etude aux chemins de fer

records.title: The LP
records.change: Columbia launches the 33⅓ rpm long-playing record, with about 23 minutes per side.
records.idea: The album: a long, ordered statement instead of single sides.

records.change: In John Cage’s piece the performer plays nothing for four minutes and 33 seconds; the music is the sound of the room.
records.idea: Silence and chance are music, and the listener completes the piece.

records.title: Rock and roll
records.change: Elvis Presley’s first single (1954) and Bill Haley’s “Rock Around the Clock”, a US No. 1 in 1955, make rhythm-and-blues-based music the sound of teenagers.
records.idea: Music as youth identity.
records.listen: Bill Haley & His Comets — Rock Around the Clock
records.q: Bill Haley Rock Around the Clock

records.title: Computer music
records.change: Max Mathews at Bell Labs writes MUSIC, the first computer program to generate digital audio.
records.idea: Music can be calculated.

records.title: A computer sings
records.change: An IBM 7090 at Bell Labs sings “Daisy Bell”, the first song sung with computer speech synthesis. HAL sings the same song in “2001: A Space Odyssey”.
records.idea: The machine gets a voice.

records.title: The protest song
records.change: Bob Dylan’s “Blowin’ in the Wind” and the anthem “We Shall Overcome” carry the US civil-rights movement.
records.idea: A song can carry a movement.
records.listen: Bob Dylan — Blowin’ in the Wind
records.q: Bob Dylan Blowin' in the Wind

records.title: The cassette
records.change: Philips launches the compact cassette, and people record and copy music at home.
records.idea: Listeners become curators: the mixtape.

records.title: The synthesizer
records.change: Robert Moog builds the first commercial modular synthesizer; the Minimoog (1970) makes it portable.
records.idea: Musicians design the sound itself, not just the notes.

records.title: Minimalism
records.change: In Terry Riley’s “In C”, each player repeats 53 short phrases at their own pace.
records.idea: Repetition and slow change can be the whole piece.

records.title: The studio as instrument
records.change: The Beatles’ “Sgt. Pepper”, built from four-track tape, loops and effects, is made for the studio rather than the stage.
records.idea: The recording itself is the artwork.
records.listen: The Beatles — A Day in the Life
records.q: The Beatles A Day in the Life

records.title: The mass festival
records.change: About half a million people gather at Woodstock in upstate New York.
records.idea: Music as a shared event for a whole generation.

records.title: The breakbeat
records.change: At a Bronx party in August 1973, DJ Kool Herc loops the drum breaks of funk records on two turntables, and hip hop grows from parties like it.
records.idea: The turntable is an instrument: new music from old records.
records.listen: Grandmaster Flash — The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel

records.title: Afrofuturism
records.change: Sun Ra’s “Space Is the Place” (album 1973, film 1974) imagines Black liberation in outer space.
records.idea: Imagine the future to change the present.
records.listen: Sun Ra — Space Is the Place
records.q: Sun Ra Space Is the Place

records.title: Man-machine pop
records.change: Kraftwerk’s “Autobahn” becomes an international hit built on synthesizers and a vocoder.
records.idea: The machine becomes the band’s identity.

records.title: Punk and do-it-yourself
records.change: Punk bands record for small labels, print their own fanzines and play with three chords.
records.idea: You do not need permission or training to make music.

records.title: I Feel Love
records.change: Giorgio Moroder builds Donna Summer’s “I Feel Love” almost entirely on a Moog synthesizer. Bowie later recalled Eno calling it the sound of the future.
records.idea: Electronic dance music begins.

records.title: The Golden Record
records.change: NASA sends a record of Earth’s music on both Voyager probes, from Bach to Chuck Berry.
records.idea: Music as humanity’s message to the far future.

records.title: Ambient music
records.change: Brian Eno’s “Music for Airports” defines ambient music as “as ignorable as it is interesting”.
records.idea: Music as the atmosphere of a place.

records.title: The Walkman
records.change: Sony’s Walkman goes on sale on 1 July 1979 and takes a private soundtrack out into the street.
records.idea: Personal listening: everyone carries their own soundtrack.

records.title: The sampler
records.change: The Fairlight CMI records any sound and plays it back at any pitch from a keyboard.
records.idea: Any recorded sound becomes an instrument.

records.title: The TR-808
records.change: Roland’s drum machine is a commercial failure, then becomes the backbone of hip hop, electro and trap.
records.idea: Cheap machines start new genres.
records.listen: Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force — Planet Rock (1982)

records.title: MTV
records.change: MTV launches with “Video Killed the Radio Star”, and songs now need a picture.
records.idea: Music becomes audiovisual.
records.listen: The Buggles — Video Killed the Radio Star
records.q: The Buggles Video Killed the Radio Star

records.title: The compact disc
records.change: The first CDs go on sale in Japan.
records.idea: Music becomes digital data.

records.title: MIDI
records.change: A shared standard lets synthesizers and computers from different makers play each other.
records.idea: Machines share one musical language.

records.title: Techno
records.change: In Detroit, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson make futuristic machine music; a 1988 UK compilation names it techno.
records.idea: Music about the future, made in a post-industrial city.

records.title: The computer studio
records.change: Digidesign’s Pro Tools turns a computer into a multitrack studio; GarageBand (2004) puts one on every Mac.
records.idea: Anyone can own a studio.

records.title: MP3
records.change: The MP3 format, developed largely at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute, shrinks audio about tenfold.
records.idea: Music becomes a file that travels over the internet.

records.title: Auto-Tune
records.change: Auto-Tune corrects pitch, and Cher’s “Believe” (1998) uses it as an audible effect.
records.idea: The machine-processed voice becomes a style.

records.title: Napster
records.change: Napster lets millions share MP3s for free, and recorded-music revenue falls for over a decade.
records.idea: Access matters more than ownership.

records.title: The iPod
records.change: Apple’s iPod promises “1,000 songs in your pocket”; the iTunes Store (2003) sells songs one at a time.
records.idea: A whole library goes everywhere.

records.title: YouTube
records.change: Anyone can upload a song or a cover and find an audience without a label.
records.idea: Distribution without gatekeepers.

records.title: Hatsune Miku
records.change: Crypton releases a Vocaloid singing voice with a character, and fans write songs for her by the thousand.
records.idea: A virtual singer anyone can write for.
records.listen: livetune feat. Hatsune Miku — Tell Your World

records.title: Streaming
records.change: Spotify launches in 2008. By 2016, streaming brings in 51% of US recorded-music revenue, the first time it is the majority.
records.idea: Every song, always, for a subscription.

records.title: AI writes in a style
records.change: Sony CSL’s Flow Machines composes “Daddy’s Car” in the style of the Beatles; composer Benoît Carré arranges it and writes the lyrics.
records.idea: A machine can learn a style and write in it.

records.title: The TikTok hit
records.change: Lil Nas X records “Old Town Road” on a beat bought online for $30. Spread on TikTok, it spends a record 19 weeks at No. 1 in the US.
records.idea: Short videos decide what becomes a hit.
records.listen: Lil Nas X — Old Town Road
records.q: Lil Nas X Old Town Road

records.title: An AI in the band
records.change: Holly Herndon’s album “PROTO” features Spawn, a neural network trained to sing with her ensemble.
records.idea: AI as a bandmate, not a replacement.

records.title: A voice others can use
records.change: Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst launch Holly+, a model of her voice that others can sing through, under rules they set.
records.idea: A voice becomes something you can license.

records.title: Avatar concerts
records.change: ABBA Voyage opens in London: the band appears as digital avatars made by Industrial Light & Magic, with a live band on stage.
records.idea: A concert without the stars in the room.

records.title: AI restores a lost voice
records.change: Machine learning separates John Lennon’s voice from a 1970s demo, and the Beatles release “Now and Then”. It wins a Grammy in 2025.
records.idea: Old recordings can be remade.

records.title: “Heart on My Sleeve”
records.change: A song with AI-cloned voices of Drake and The Weeknd goes viral and is pulled from streaming services within days.
records.idea: Who owns a voice?

records.title: Songs from a sentence
records.change: Suno and Udio generate full songs with vocals from a text prompt. Major labels sue both in 2024; in late 2025 Universal and Warner settle and sign licensing deals.
records.idea: You can compose by describing.

forecasts.title: Music that adapts to you
forecasts.text: Soundtracks generated for one listener, place and moment become ordinary, the way Eno’s generative apps already work.

forecasts.title: Voices and catalogues as licences
forecasts.text: Artists opt in to let AI use their voice and songs and are paid per use, as in Holly+ and the 2025 label deals.

forecasts.title: Everyone composes
forecasts.text: Describing a song is enough to make one. Skill moves to taste, editing and performance.

forecasts.title: Being there becomes the scarce part
forecasts.text: Recorded music is unlimited, so shared live moments with musicians, avatars and a crowd carry the value.

forecasts.title: Machines as bandmates
forecasts.text: Playing with an AI musician that listens and answers is as normal as playing with a drum machine.
